newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe's Mugabe urges world solar energy pledge.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe's Mugabe urges world solar energy pledge.

text.p: Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe urged world leaders on Saturday to help bring two billion people condemned to a life without electricity into the modern world by promoting the use of solar power.

Opening a preparatory meeting ahead of a two-day World Solar Summit opening on Monday, Mugabe said he was dismayed that despite some strides in developing solar technology, it was under-utilised compared to other forms of energy.

"All the technologies that we can develop and transfer, or all the funding that we can provide, indeed all our efforts to promote the development and use of solar energy will bear few tangible results without the necessary political will," he said.

About 14 world leaders, including Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and South African President Nelson Mandela, were invite to attend the Saturday meeting but only two turned up -- Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohammad and Pakistani President Farooq Leghari.
Mugabe called for greater use of renewable energy resources, pointing to growing international concern about global warming, deforestation and widespread and frequent droughts.

He also lamented the disparity in energy use worldwide, saying that developing countries, where 79 percent of the world's population lived, accounted for only 30 percent of global consumption while developed countries, home to 21 percent of the world's population, consumed 70 percent of the commercial energy produced globally.
In southern Africa for example, non-convential energy sources such as wood-fuel, charcoal and crop residues, accounted for almost 80 percent of the region's average energy demands, he said.

"This goes to confirm how dependent developing countries are on non-conventional forms of energy at a time when the encroachment of drought, agriculture and other human activities have resulted in the loss of biomass," he said.

Frederico Mayor, director-general of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) which is jointly organising the two-day solar summit, said the exclusion of millions of people from modern life could breed extremism and promote instability.
